court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department
holding_summary: A rent-stabilized tenant who sublet her apartment to 93 different Airbnb guests over 338 days across 18 months, charging nightly rates far exceeding the lawful 10% sublet premium, engaged in unlawful profiteering as a matter of law. Because the conduct was sustained and substantial rather than isolated, she was not entitled to a right to cure, and the landlord was entitled to terminate the lease and evict her.

quotes.text: the record establishes that defendant’s “guests” were, as a matter of law, subtenants, and this matter is therefore governed by RSC § 2525.6
defendant’s systematic commercial exploitation of her rent-stabilized leasehold fully warrants the termination of her lease.
Turning her rent-stabilized apartment into a single-unit tourist hotel in this fashion enabled defendant to earn substantial profits, far in excess of the legally permissible 10% premium.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department
holding_summary: A restrictive covenant barring 'business' use — defined to include operating a hotel or boarding/lodging house and housing paying guests for profit — does not bar a homeowner from leasing his or her entire home to a tenant on an ordinary lease. Because the covenant contemplates the possibility of leasing (by barring both owners and tenants from business use) and does not expressly prohibit residential leasing, a two-year lease of the defendants' home did not violate it.

quotes.text: the subject covenant prohibits any “owner, tenant or occupant” of premises located in Edgewater Point from operating a boarding or lodging house for paying guests. However, the covenant does not expressly bar a property owner from leasing his or her home, and, in fact, contemplates the possibility that homes will be leased by barring both tenants and owners from using premises for business purposes.
It is well settled that the law favors the free and unobstructed use of real property
the Supreme Court properly dismissed the complaint on the ground that the restrictive covenant does not bar an Edgewater Point property owner from leasing his or her home.

holding_summary: In a companion zoning-enforcement action, the court held that a cottage containing a bathroom and two bedrooms, moved onto defendants' lot and given a permanent foundation, violated the town's single-family zoning ordinance's ban on accessory structures containing 'living quarters.' The court reasoned the ordinance validly confined each lot to one household, a concern it linked to the tourist area's pattern of short-term rental of extra living quarters, and ordered the cottage removed.

quotes.text: No accessory structure having living quarters is permitted.

The obvious legislative planning scheme in the ordinance is the recognition of residential control over a household unit in one building with all rooms accessible from inside. What is prohibited in the ordinance are separate buildings with living quarters. The reason is obvious especially in this tourist area where high rents and overnight and weekend occupancy are common with or without kitchen facilities.
